### V-278917 · UBTU-24-700400 · CAT I: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must be a vendor-supported release.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-278917r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Patching & Supported Software |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be a vendor-supported release.

**Why it matters:** Software makers regularly release fixes for security holes they discover. This rule requires installing those fixes and only running versions that are still supported. It's like getting the recall repair on your car: skip it, and the known problem stays there for anyone to take advantage of.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION /etc/lsb-release
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
pro status
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Patch from approved repositories with 'apt-get update && apt-get upgrade' (or 'unattended-upgrades' for automatic security updates). Review pending updates with 'apt list --upgradable'. Check the release with 'lsb_release -a' against Canonical's support lifecycle; an Ubuntu Pro subscription extends security maintenance (ESM).

**Operational impact:** Patching requires maintenance windows and sometimes reboots. Test critical applications against updates in a staging environment, but don't let testing stretch beyond IAVM deadlines.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is vendor supported with the following command:

$ grep DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION /etc/lsb-release
DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION="Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS"

Check the subscription status of the system with the following command:
$ pro status

If the installed version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is not supported, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Upgrade to a supported version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An operating system release is considered "supported" if the vendor continues to provide security patches for the product. With an unsupported release, it will not be possible to resolve security issues discovered in the system software.

The support status of the OS depends on its subscription status.

End Of Life dates for Ubuntu 24.04 releases are as follows:
Standard Support: April 2029
Extended Security Maintenance (ESM): April 2036

ESM is available via an Ubuntu Pro subscription.

**Threat & control context:** Known, unpatched vulnerabilities remain the most common initial-access and privilege-escalation vector. Running an unsupported release means new vulnerabilities will never be fixed. SI-2 (flaw remediation) and SA-22 (unsupported system components) require timely patching per organizational timelines (IAVM compliance in DoD) and replacement of end-of-life components. Unsupported OS findings are CAT I because they can't be mitigated by configuration alone.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

#### Level 3: General Audience

It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | -R 0640 /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/* |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo ls -al /etc/audit/ /etc/audit/rules.d/
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

```text
sudo stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /etc/audit/rules.d/*
```

Expected: Mode/owner/group must match: chmod -R 0640 /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/*.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify /etc/audit/audit.rules, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, and /etc/audit/auditd.conf files have a mode of "0640" or less permissive with the following command:

$ sudo ls -al /etc/audit/ /etc/audit/rules.d/
/etc/audit/:

-rw-r-----   1 root root   804 Nov 25 11:01 auditd.conf
 -rw-r-----   1 root root  9128 Dec 27 09:56 audit.rules
-rw-r-----   1 root root   127 Feb  7  2018 audit-stop.rules

drwxr-x---   2 root root  4096 Dec 27 09:56 rules.d

/etc/audit/rules.d/:

 -rw-r----- 1 root root 244 Dec 27 09:56 audit.rules
-rw-r----- 1 root root 10357 Dec 27 09:56 stig.rules

If /etc/audit/audit.rule, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, or /etc/audit/auditd.conf files have a mode more permissive than "0640", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure /etc/audit/audit.rules, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, and /etc/audit/auditd.conf files to have a mode of "0640" by using the following command:

$ sudo chmod -R 0640 /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/*
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to restrict which roles and individuals can select which events are audited, unauthorized personnel may be able to prevent the auditing of critical events.

Misconfigured audits may degrade the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfigured audits may also make it more difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000171**: Allow organization-defined personnel or roles to select the event types that are to be logged by specific components of the system.

### V-270776 · UBTU-24-900050 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must permit only authorized accounts to own the audit configuration files.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270776r1066817_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000063-GPOS-00032 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000171 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 b |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must permit only authorized accounts to own the audit configuration files.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chown | root /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/* |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo ls -al /etc/audit/ /etc/audit/rules.d/
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /etc/audit/rules.d/*
```

Expected: Mode/owner/group must match: chown root /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/*.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify /etc/audit/audit.rules, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, and /etc/audit/auditd.conf files are owned by "root" account with the following command:

$ sudo ls -al /etc/audit/ /etc/audit/rules.d/
/etc/audit/:

-rw-r-----   1 root root   804 Nov 25 11:01 auditd.conf
 -rw-r-----   1 root root  9128 Dec 27 09:56 audit.rules
-rw-r-----   1 root root   127 Feb  7  2018 audit-stop.rules

drwxr-x---   2 root root  4096 Dec 27 09:56 rules.d

/etc/audit/rules.d/:

 -rw-r----- 1 root root 244 Dec 27 09:56 audit.rules
-rw-r----- 1 root root 10357 Dec 27 09:56 stig.rules

If the /etc/audit/audit.rules, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, or /etc/audit/auditd.conf file is owned by a user other than "root", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure /etc/audit/audit.rules, /etc/audit/rules.d/*, and /etc/audit/auditd.conf files to be owned by "root" user by using the following command:

$ sudo chown root /etc/audit/audit*.{rules,conf} /etc/audit/rules.d/*
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to restrict which roles and individuals can select which events are audited, unauthorized personnel may be able to prevent the auditing of critical events.

Misconfigured audits may degrade the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfigured audits may also make it more difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000171**: Allow organization-defined personnel or roles to select the event types that are to be logged by specific components of the system.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 b · Rev 4: AU-12 b · Rev 3: AU-12 b

### V-270778 · UBTU-24-900070 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the su command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270778r1066823_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the su command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-priv_change |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep /bin/su
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/bin/su'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-priv_change

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "su" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /bin/su
-a always,exit -F path=/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-priv_change

If the command does not return lines that match the example or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 24.04 LTS to generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "su" command occur.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-priv_change

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records that are specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the umount command.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/umount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-umount |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/umount
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/umount'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/umount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-umount

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "umount" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/umount
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/umount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-umount

If the command does not return lines that match the example or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "umount" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/umount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-umount

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

| Field | Value |

| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the ssh-agent command.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-ssh |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/ssh-agent
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/ssh-agent'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-ssh

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and, on 22.04 and later, drop-ins in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf, which are included at the top of the main file so their values take precedence (first value wins). Validate with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload ssh' (the unit is named 'ssh' on Ubuntu).

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates an audit record upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "ssh-agent" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/ssh-agent
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-ssh

If the command does not return lines that match the example or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "ssh-agent" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-ssh

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. - **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.

Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates an audit record upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "chown", "fchown", "fchownat", and "lchown" system calls with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep chown
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S chown,fchown,fchownat,lchown -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S chown,fchown,fchownat,lchown -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng

If the command does not return audit rules for the "chown", "fchown", "fchownat", and "lchown" syscalls or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.

Notes:
- For 32-bit architectures, only the 32-bit specific output lines from the commands are required.
- The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "chown", "fchown", "fchownat", and "lchown" system calls.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S chown,fchown,fchownat,lchown -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S chown,fchown,fchownat,lchown -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng

Note: For 32-bit architectures, only the 32-bit specific entries are required.

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall that all programs on the system makes. Therefore, it is very important to only use syscall rules when absolutely necessary since these affect performance. The more rules, the bigger the performance hit. The performance is helped, though, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

### V-270788 · UBTU-24-900170 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the sudo command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270788r1066853_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the sudo command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudo -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/sudo
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/sudo'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudo -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify an audit event is generated for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "sudo" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/sudo
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudo -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

If the command does not return a line that matches the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "sudo" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudo -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "sudoedit" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudoedit -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-270790 · UBTU-24-900190 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the chsh command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270790r1068380_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the chsh command.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep chsh
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/chsh'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates an audit record upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "chsh" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep chsh
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

If the command does not return a line that matches the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "chsh" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k priv_cmd

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chacl -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
audtctl -l | grep chacl
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text

```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chacl -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k perm_chng

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

```text

If the command does not return a line that matches the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that an audit event is generated for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "gpasswd" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep -w gpasswd
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/gpasswd -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-gpasswd

If the command does not return a line that matches the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful uses of the "gpasswd" command.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/gpasswd -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-gpasswd

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/pam_timestamp_check -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k privileged-pam_timestamp_check

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. ### V-270807 · UBTU-24-900510 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to modify the /etc/sudoers file occur.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270807r1066910_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to modify the /etc/sudoers file occur.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege_modification |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep sudoers
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/etc/sudoers'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege_modification

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates audit records for all modifications that affect "/etc/sudoers" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep sudoers
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege_modification

If the command does not return a line that matches the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 24.04 LTS to generate audit records for all modifications that affect "/etc/sudoers".

Add or update the following rule to "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules":

-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege_modification

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for any successful/unsuccessful use of unlink, unlinkat, rename, renameat, and rmdir system calls.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k delete |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k delete |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep 'unlink\|rename\|rmdir'
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- 'unlink'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k delete

**How it works:** Lock the root password ('passwd -l root') so administrators work through sudo, set 'PermitRootLogin no' and 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd, and remove 'nullok' from pam_unix in /etc/pam.d/common-auth and common-password so empty passwords are rejected.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates audit records for any successful/unsuccessful use of "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" system calls with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep 'unlink\|rename\|rmdir'
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=delete
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=delete

If the command does not return audit rules for the "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" syscalls or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.

Notes:
- For 32-bit architectures, only the 32-bit specific output lines from the commands are required.
- The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate audit events for any successful/unsuccessful use of "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" system calls.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k delete
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k delete

Note: For 32-bit architectures, only the 32-bit specific entries are required.

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall that all programs on the system makes. Therefore, it is very important to only use syscall rules when absolutely necessary since these affect performance. The more rules, the bigger the performance hit. The performance is helped, though, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-270810 · UBTU-24-900590 · CAT II: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must generate audit records for the /var/log/wtmp file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270810r1066919_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000472-GPOS-00217 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for the /var/log/wtmp file.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules | -w /var/log/wtmp -p wa -k logins |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep '/var/log/wtmp'
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/var/log/wtmp'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -w /var/log/wtmp -p wa -k logins

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On Ubuntu, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS generates audit records showing start and stop times for user access to the system via the "/var/log/wtmp" file with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep '/var/log/wtmp'
-w /var/log/wtmp -p wa -k logins

If the command does not return a line matching the example or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the audit system to generate audit events showing start and stop times for user access via the "/var/log/wtmp" file.

Add or update the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-w /var/log/wtmp -p wa -k logins

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is configured to audit the execution of the module management program "kmod" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep kmod
-w /bin/kmod -p x -k module

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Note: The "-k" allows for specifying an arbitrary identifier, and the string after it does not need to match the example output above.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 24.04 LTS to audit the execution of the module management program "kmod".

Add or update the following rule in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/stig.rules" file:

-w /bin/kmod -p x -k modules

To reload the rules file, issue the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

### V-270816 · UBTU-24-900920 · CAT III: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS must allocate audit record storage capacity to store at least one week's worth of audit records, when audit records are not immediately sent to a central audit record storage facility.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-270816r1066937_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000341-GPOS-00132 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001849 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must allocate audit record storage capacity to store at least one week's worth of audit records, when audit records are not immediately sent to a central audit record storage facility.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep ^log_file /etc/audit/auditd.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
df -h /var/log/audit/
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
du -sh [audit_partition]
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS allocates audit record storage capacity to store at least one week's worth of audit records when audit records are not immediately sent to a central audit record storage facility.

Determine which partition the audit records are being written to with the following command:

$ sudo grep ^log_file /etc/audit/auditd.conf
log_file = /var/log/audit/audit.log

Check the size of the partition that audit records are written to (with the example being "/var/log/audit/") with the following command:

$ sudo df -h /var/log/audit/
/dev/sda2 24G 10.4G 13.6G 43% /var/log/audit

If the audit records are not written to a partition made specifically for audit records ("/var/log/audit" is a separate partition), determine the amount of space being used by other files in the partition with the following command:

$ sudo du -sh [audit_partition]
1.8G /var/log/audit

Note: The partition size needed to capture a week's worth of audit records is based on the activity level of the system and the total storage capacity available.

If the audit record partition is not allocated for sufficient storage capacity, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Allocate enough storage capacity for at least one week's worth of audit records when audit records are not immediately sent to a central audit record storage facility.

If audit records are stored on a partition made specifically for audit records, use the "parted" program to resize the partition with sufficient space to contain one week's worth of audit records.

If audit records are not stored on a partition made specifically for audit records, a new partition with sufficient amount of space will need be to be created.

Set the auditd server to point to the mount point where the audit records must be located:

$ sudo sed -i -E 's@^(log_file\s*=\s*).*@\1 <log mountpoint>/audit.log@' /etc/audit/auditd.conf

where <log mountpoint> is the aforementioned mount point.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure operating systems have a sufficient storage capacity in which to write the audit logs, operating systems must be able to allocate audit record storage capacity.

The task of allocating audit record storage capacity is usually performed during initial installation of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001849**: Allocate audit log storage capacity to accommodate organization-defined audit log retention requirements.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 · Rev 4: AU-4 · Rev 3: n/a

**How it works:** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 24.04 LTS notifies the SA and ISSO (at a minimum) when allocated audit record storage volume reaches 75 percent of the repository maximum audit record storage capacity with the following command:

Note: If the space_left_action is set to "email", an email package must be available.

$ sudo grep ^space_left_action /etc/audit/auditd.conf
space_left_action email

$ sudo grep ^space_left /etc/audit/auditd.conf
space_left 250000

If the "space_left" parameter is set to "syslog", is missing, set to blanks, or set to a value less than 25 percent of the space free in the allocated audit record storage, this is a finding.

If the "space_left_action" parameter is missing or set to blanks, this is a finding.

If the "space_left_action" is set to "email", check the value of the "action_mail_acct" parameter with the following command:

$ sudo grep ^action_mail_acct /etc/audit/auditd.conf
action_mail_acct root@localhost

The "action_mail_acct" parameter, if missing, defaults to "root". If the "action_mail_acct parameter" is not set to the email address of the SA(s) and/or ISSO, this is a finding.

If the "space_left_action" is set to "exec", the system executes a designated script. If this script informs the SA of the event, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Edit "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" and set the "space_left_action" parameter to "exec" or "email".

If the "space_left_action" parameter is set to "email", set the "action_mail_acct" parameter to an email address for the SA and ISSO.

If the "space_left_action" parameter is set to "exec", ensure the command being executed notifies the SA and ISSO.

Edit "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" and set the "space_left" parameter to be at least 25 percent of the repository maximum audit record storage capacity.
```

AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001855**: Provide a warning to organization-defined personnel, roles, and/or locations within an organization-defined time period when allocated audit log storage volume reaches an organization-defined percentage of repository maximum audit log storage capacity.  
  Rev 5: AU-5 (1) · Rev 4: AU-5 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the SA and ISSO (at a minimum) are notified in the event of an audit processing failure with the following command:

$ sudo grep '^action_mail_acct' /etc/audit/auditd.conf
action_mail_acct = <administrator_account>

If the value of the "action_mail_acct" keyword is not set to an account for security personnel, the returned line is commented out, or the keyword is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure "auditd" service to notify the SA and ISSO in the event of an audit processing failure.

Edit the following line in "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" to ensure administrators are notified via email for those situations:

action_mail_acct = <administrator_account>

Note: Change "administrator_account" to an account for security personnel.

Restart the "auditd" service so the changes take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart auditd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** It is critical for the appropriate personnel to be aware if a system is at risk of failing to process audit logs as required. Without this notification, the security personnel may be unaware of an impending failure of the audit capability, and system operation may be adversely affected.

Audit processing failures include software/hardware errors, failures in the audit capturing mechanisms, and audit storage capacity being reached or exceeded.

This requirement applies to each audit data storage repository (i.e., distinct information system component where audit records are stored), the centralized audit storage capacity of organizations (i.e., all audit data storage repositories combined), or both.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000139**: Alert organization-defined personnel or roles within an organization-defined time period in the event of an audit logging process failure.  
  Rev 5: AU-5 a · Rev 4: AU-5 a · Rev 3: AU-5 a
